Senses.definition: to move or go with someone or something from one place to another
examples: Barney took us to the airport.
Would you mind taking Susie home ?
When he refused to give his name, he was taken into custody.
My job has taken me all over the world.
His wife went to Australia, taking the children with her.
I have to take Steve the money tonight.
He took me to meet his parents.

Senses.definition: used with a noun instead of using a verb to describe an action. For example, if you take a walk, you walk somewhere
examples: Would you like to take a look?
Mike’s just taking a shower.
Sara took a deep breath.
I waved, but he didn’t take any notice (= pretended not to notice ) . British English
Please take a seat (= sit down ) .
Would you mind taking a photo of us together?

Senses.definition: to remove something from a place
examples: Take your feet off the seats.
Someone’s taken a pen from my desk.
Police say money and jewellery were taken in the raid.

Senses.definition: if something takes a particular amount of time, money, effort etc, that amount of time etc is needed for it to happen or succeed
examples: How long is this going to take ?
Organizing a successful street party takes a lot of energy.
Repairs take time to carry out.
It took a few minutes for his eyes to adjust to the dark.
It took me ages to find a present for Dad.
Catching up four goals will take some doing.
It takes courage to admit you are wrong.
Neil’s got what it takes to be a great footballer.

Senses.definition: to accept or choose something that is offered, suggested, or given to you
examples: Will you take the job?
Do you take American Express?
If you take my advice , you’ll see a doctor.
Our helpline takes 3.5 million calls (= telephone calls ) a year.
Some doctors are unwilling to take new patients without a referral.
Liz found his criticisms hard to take .
I just can’t take any more (= can’t deal with a bad situation any longer ) .
Staff have agreed to take a 2% pay cut.
Small businesses took a hammering in the last recession.
That’s the truth – take it from me .
He’s the kind of man who makes things happen but lets others take the credit.
It isn’t official yet, but you can take it as read that you’ve got the contract.

Senses.definition: to get hold of something in your hands
examples: Let me take your coat.
Can you take this package while I get my wallet?
I just wanted to take him in my arms.

Senses.definition: to use a particular form of transport or a particular road in order to go somewhere
examples: Let’s take a cab.
I took the first plane out.
Take the M6 to Junction 19.

Senses.definition: to study a particular subject in school or college for an examination
examples: Are you taking French next year?

Senses.definition: to do an examination or test
examples: Applicants are asked to take a written test.

Senses.definition: to be the correct or suitable size, type etc for a particular person or thing
examples: a car that takes low sulphur fuel
What size shoe do you take?
The elevator takes a maximum of 32 people.
· I take size 12.

Senses.definition: to collect or gather something for a particular purpose
examples: Investigators will take samples of the wreckage to identify the cause.
The police took a statement from both witnesses.

Senses.definition: to react to someone or something or consider them in a particular way
examples: I was joking, but he took me seriously.
Ben took the news very badly.
She does not take kindly to criticism (= reacts badly to criticism ) .
I’ll take that remark as a compliment.
The presence of dust clouds has been taken as evidence of recent star formation.
I took her to be his daughter.
Of course I won’t tell anyone! What do you take me for ? (= what sort of person do you think I am? )
I take it (= I assume ) you’ve heard that Rick’s resigned.

Senses.definition: to have or experience a particular feeling
examples: You should take pride in your work.
At first, he took no interest in the baby.
She stood feeling lost until an elderly man took pity on her.
Don’t take offence. Roger says things like that to everybody.
Investors can take comfort from the fact that the World Bank is underwriting the shares.

Senses.definition: to get possession or control of something
examples: Enemy forces have taken the airport.
Both boys were taken prisoner .
The communists took power in 1948.
Youngsters need to take control of their own lives.

Senses.definition: to swallow, breathe in, inject etc a drug or medicine
examples: The doctor will ask whether you are taking any medication.
Take two tablets before bedtime.
Most teenagers start taking drugs through boredom.
She took an overdose after a row with her boyfriend.

Senses.definition: used to ask someone whether they like to have sugar or milk in a drink such as tea or coffee
to make someone or something go to a higher level or position
examples: The latest raise takes his salary into six figures.
Even if you have the talent to take you to the top , there’s no guarantee you’ll get there.
If you want to take it further , you should consult an attorney.

Senses.definition: to measure the amount, level, rate etc of something
examples: Take the patient’s pulse first.

Senses.definition: to make a number smaller by a particular amount
examples: ‘Take four from nine and what do you get?’ ‘Five.’
Ten take away nine equals one.

Senses.definition: if a shop, business etc takes a particular amount of money, it receives that amount of money from its customers
examples: The stall took £25 on Saturday.

Senses.definition: to neither like nor dislike something
examples: To some people, smoking is addictive. Others can take it or leave it.

Senses.definition: used to give an example of something you have just been talking about
examples: People love British cars. Take the Mini. In Japan, it still sells more than all the other British cars put together.

Senses.definition: to teach a particular group of students in a school or college
examples: Who takes you for English?

Senses.definition: to write down information
examples: Let me take your email address.
Sue offered to take notes .

Senses.definition: to make someone forget their problems and feel more confident
examples: Alf said joining the club would take me out of myself.

Senses.definition: to make you very tired
examples: Looking after a baby really takes it out of you.

Senses.definition: to decide to do something without getting someone’s permission or approval first
examples: Reg took it upon himself to hand the press a list of names.

Senses.definition: to separate something into its different parts
examples: how to take an engine to bits

Senses.definition: to be attracted by a particular idea, plan, or person
examples: I’m quite taken by the idea of Christmas in Berlin.

Senses.definition: to suddenly become ill
if a man takes someone, he has sex with them
to try to get over or around something in a particular way
examples: He took the bend at over 60 and lost control.

Senses.definition: if a treatment, dye , drug etc takes, it begins to work successfully
to be very surprised about something
examples: Emma was somewhat taken aback by his directness.

Senses.definition: to look or behave like an older relative
examples: Jenni really takes after her mother.

Senses.definition: to separate something into all its different parts
examples: Tom was always taking things apart in the garage.

Senses.definition: to search a place very thoroughly
examples: The police took the house apart looking for clues.

Senses.definition: to beat someone very easily in a game, sport, fight etc
to show that someone is wrong or something is not true
examples: Tariq takes several gay myths apart in his book.

Senses.definition: to begin to dislike someone or something, especially without a good reason
examples: Voters took against the relationship between the government and the unions in the 1970s.

Senses.definition: to remove someone or something, or make something disappear
examples: She whisked the tray off the table and took it away.
He was taken away to begin a prison sentence.
This should take some of the pain away.

Senses.definition: if you buy food to take away, you buy cooked food from a restaurant and take it outside to eat it somewhere else
examples: Fish and chips to take away, please.

Senses.definition: to be very beautiful, exciting, or surprising
to spoil the good effect or success that something has
examples: The disagreement between the two men should not take away from their accomplishments.

Senses.definition: to admit that you were wrong to say something
examples: You’d better take back that remark!

Senses.definition: to take something you have bought back to a shop because it is not suitable
examples: If the shirt doesn’t fit, take it back.

Senses.definition: to make you remember a time in the past
examples: Having the grandchildren around takes me back to the days when my own children were small.

Senses.definition: to move something that is fixed in a high position to a lower position
examples: She made us take down all the posters.

Senses.definition: to write down information
examples: Can I just take some details down?

Senses.definition: to pull a piece of clothing such as trousers part of the way down your legs
to be completely deceived by someone who lies to you
examples: Don’t be taken in by products claiming to help you lose weight in a week.

Senses.definition: to let someone stay in your house because they have nowhere else to stay
examples: Brett’s always taking in stray animals.

Senses.definition: to understand and remember new facts and information
examples: He watches the older kids, just taking it all in.
His eyes quickly took in the elegance of her dress.

Senses.definition: to collect or earn a particular amount of money
to visit a place while you are in the area
examples: They continued a few miles further to take in Hinton House.

Senses.definition: if you take in a show, play etc, you go to see it
if the police take someone in, they take them to a police station to ask them questions about a crime
examples: All five teenagers were arrested and taken in for questioning .

Senses.definition: to make a piece of clothing fit you by making it narrower
to remove a piece of clothing
examples: He sat on the bed to take his boots off.
Charlie was taking off his shirt when the phone rang.

Senses.definition: if an aircraft takes off, it rises into the air from the ground
examples: I felt quite excited as the plane took off from Heathrow.

Senses.definition: to suddenly start being successful
examples: Mimi became jealous when Jack’s career started taking off .

Senses.definition: to have a holiday from work on a particular day, or for a particular length of time
examples: I rang my boss and arranged to take some time off.
Dad took the day off to come with me.

Senses.definition: to copy the way someone speaks or behaves, in order to entertain people
to start to employ someone
examples: We’re taking on 50 new staff this year.

Senses.definition: to agree to do some work or be responsible for something
examples: Don’t take on too much work – the extra cash isn’t worth it.

Senses.definition: to begin to have a particular quality or appearance
examples: Her face took on a fierce expression.
His life had taken on a new dimension.

Senses.definition: to compete against someone or start a fight with someone, especially someone bigger or better than you
examples: Nigeria will take on Argentina in the first round of the World Cup on Saturday.
He was prepared to take on anyone who laid a finger on us.

Senses.definition: if a plane or ship takes on people or things, they come onto it
examples: We stopped to take on fuel.

Senses.definition: to take someone as your guest to a restaurant, cinema, club etc
examples: We’re taking my folks out for a meal next week.

Senses.definition: to make a financial or legal arrangement with a bank, company, law court etc
examples: Before taking a loan out, calculate your monthly outgoings.

Senses.definition: to get money from your bank account
examples: How much would you like to take out?

Senses.definition: to borrow books from a library
examples: You can take out six books at a time.

Senses.definition: to kill someone or destroy something
examples: The building was taken out by a bomb.

Senses.definition: to treat someone badly when you are angry or upset, even though it is not their fault
examples: Don’t take it out on me just because you’ve had a bad day.
Irritated with herself, she took her annoyance out on Bridget.

Senses.definition: to take control of something
examples: His only reason for investing in the company was to take it over.
Ruth moved into our apartment and promptly took over.

Senses.definition: to start to like someone or something
examples: Sandra took to it straight away .
Charles was an odd character whom Kelly had never really taken to.

Senses.definition: to start doing something regularly
examples: Dee’s taken to getting up at 6 and going jogging.

Senses.definition: to get into your bed and stay there
examples: He was so depressed, he took to his bed for a week.

Senses.definition: to become interested in a new activity and to spend time doing it
examples: Roger took painting up for a while, but soon lost interest.

Senses.definition: to start a new job or have a new responsibility
examples: Peter will take up the management of the finance department.
The headteacher takes up her duties in August.

Senses.definition: if you take up a suggestion, problem, complaint etc, you start to do something about it
examples: Now the papers have taken up the story.
The hospital manager has promised to take the matter up with the member of staff involved.
I am still very angry and will be taking it up with the authorities.

Senses.definition: to fill a particular amount of time or space
examples: The little time I had outside of school was taken up with work.
old books that were taking up space in the office

Senses.definition: to accept a suggestion, offer, or idea
examples: Rob took up the invitation to visit.
Rick took up the challenge and cycled the 250-mile route alone.

Senses.definition: to move to the exact place where you should be, so that you are ready to do something
examples: The runners are taking up their positions on the starting line.

Senses.definition: to make a piece of clothing shorter
to continue a story or activity that you or someone else had begun, after a short break
examples: I’ll take up the story where you left off.

Senses.definition: to accept an invitation or suggestion
examples: I’ll take you up on that offer of a drink, if it still stands.

Senses.definition: to become friendly with someone, especially someone who may influence you badly
